subject: ELA
overview: Teach phonics daily in a short, explicit routine (model, practice with tiles or cards, read words in sentences), then spend the rest of the hour reading aloud and writing. Read the named books aloud yourself first, ask the text-based questions, and let your child retell before they write. Score weekly checks gently, note patterns your child misses, and reteach those patterns in the next week's warm-ups.

weeks.prep: Gather letter tiles or magnetic letters, primary-lined paper, a printed copy of 'Hey Diddle Diddle' (Mother Goose, Project Gutenberg), 'Chrysanthemum' by Kevin Henkes from the library, and a list of 10 short-a words (cat, map, bag, sat, hat, man, pan, dad, rag, ham). Preview 'Chrysanthemum' — it deals gently with teasing about a name.
misconceptions: Writing a sentence without a capital or period: say 'Every sentence starts with a capital and stops with a period' and have your child point to both in every sentence they write.
Reading CVC words by guessing from the first letter (cat → 'cup'): have your child touch and say each sound, then slide a finger under the word to blend.
Confusing letters and words when pointing: frame each word with two fingers and count the words in a line together.

days.guide: Read 'Hey Diddle Diddle' aloud, pointing under each word as you read so your child sees that words are read left to right with spaces between. Then show three printed sentences; your child circles the capital letter at the start and the period at the end of each.

questions.q: In 'Hey Diddle Diddle,' what jumped over the moon?
Who ran away with the spoon?
In 'The dog ran.', where is the capital and where is the period?
questions.a: The capital T at the start of The; the period after ran.

days.guide: Say cat slowly, stretching the middle: /c/ /ă/ /t/, and ask which sound is in the middle. Your child builds cat with tiles, then swaps the first tile to make mat, sat, hat, reading each word by touching each tile and blending.

questions.q: What is the middle sound in map?
Change the c in cat to h. What word?

days.guide: Model lowercase a, c, d as 'circle letters': start at the 2 o'clock position and curve back around. Your child writes each letter 5 times, then writes bad, cad, dad, leaving a finger space between words.

questions.q: Where do you start a lowercase c?
questions.a: Just below the top line on the right side (2 o'clock), curving back around to the left.

questions.q: Which letter is a circle plus a tall line: a or d?
questions.a: d — its line goes up to the top line.

days.guide: Review three listening rules: take turns, look at the speaker, ask a question. Read 'Chrysanthemum' and stop when the girls tease her name to ask how she feels. Your child asks you one question about her name.

questions.q: How does Chrysanthemum feel about her name at the start of the story?
questions.a: She loves it; she thinks it is perfect.

questions.q: Why does her name start to bother her at school?
questions.a: Other children (led by Victoria) laugh at it because it is long — it has 13 letters — and is the name of a flower.

questions.q: What makes her love her name again?
questions.a: The music teacher, Mrs. Twinkle, says her own name is long too and she will name her baby Chrysanthemum.

days.guide: Your child reads the 10 short-a words while you tally correct words. Then dictate 'The cat sat.' slowly, reminding them to start with a capital and end with a period.

questions.a: ham, pan, rag (each with short a).

weeks.assessment_key: Oral CVC check: 10 short-a words (cat, map, bag, sat, hat, man, pan, dad, rag, ham) — goal 8/10 read correctly by blending. Dictated sentence: 'The cat sat.' — 1 point capital T, 1 point correct spelling of cat and sat, 1 point period, 1 point spaces between words. Proficient = 8/10 words and 4/4 on the sentence.

weeks.prep: Index cards for sight words (the, a, is, I, see, my), Elkonin sound-box strips (3 boxes drawn in a row) with 3 counters, 'The Snowy Day' by Ezra Jack Keats, a Starfall short a/i reader (starfall.com), and 12 picture cards (cat, pig, bag, pin, hat, fish, map, lip, van, wig, ham, six).
misconceptions: Spelling pig as 'pg' (dropping the vowel): push a counter for every sound in the sound boxes — every word needs a vowel.
Sounding out sight words letter by letter (t-h-e): explain 'the' is a heart word we learn by heart; practice it in many quick reads.
Confusing short a and short i: use mouth cues — /ă/ has a wide-open mouth like a yawning 'apple,' /ĭ/ is a small 'itchy' smile.

days.guide: Say pig. Push one counter into a box for each sound: /p/ /ĭ/ /g/. Your child does sit, lip, win, then writes a letter in each box.
Write the, a, is, I, see, my on two sets of cards and play Go Fish, reading each card asked for. Then read sentences like 'I see a pig.' with your child pointing to each word.

questions.q: Which word in 'The pig is big' is a sight word?

days.guide: Read 'The Snowy Day.' Afterward ask who, what, and where questions, then your child draws their favorite part.

questions.q: Who is the main character and where does the story happen?
questions.a: Peter, in his city neighborhood covered with snow.

questions.q: What happened to the snowball Peter put in his pocket?
questions.a: It melted, and the pocket was empty.

questions.q: Name two things Peter did in the snow.
questions.a: Examples: made tracks with toes in and out, dragged a stick, knocked snow off a tree, made a snow angel, slid down a snow hill.

days.guide: Model i, t, l as 'straight-line letters' that start at the top. Your child writes each 5 times, then writes tip, lit, it, sit.

questions.q: Which letter crosses: t or l?
questions.a: t has a short cross line.

questions.q: What goes on top of the i?

days.guide: Your child reads the Starfall short a/i text aloud, then sorts the 12 picture cards under 'a' or 'i' by middle sound. Finish by reading the 6 sight words.

questions.a: a: hat, map; i: fish, wig.

questions.q: What is the middle sound in six?

weeks.assessment_key: Picture sort key: short a — cat, bag, hat, map, van, ham; short i — pig, pin, fish, lip, wig, six. Proficient = 11–12 correct. Sight words: the, a, is, I, see, my — proficient = all 6 read within about 3 seconds each.

weeks.prep: Letter tiles, drawing paper, 'Owl Moon' by Jane Yolen (library), 8 spelling words (hot, mop, top, dot, bug, sun, cup, run), and a mixed short-vowel list (cat, pig, hot, bug, map, sit, top, rub).
misconceptions: Mixing short o and short u (hot → 'hut'): o is a round 'oh-oh' mouth /ŏ/; u is a relaxed grunt /ŭ/ — say pairs like hot/hut, cot/cut.
Retelling a small moment as a list of everything that happened all summer: focus on one short event (like jumping in a pool) with a beginning and end.
Changing more than one letter in word chains: say the new word, ask which sound changed, then swap just that tile.

days.guide: Build hot, pot, dot, mop, top with tiles and read them. Then play the chain: hot → hop (change last letter) → hip (change vowel). Your child says which sound changed each time.

questions.q: Change hot to hop. Which letter changed?
questions.a: The last letter: t became p.
pot, mop, top — each with short o.

days.guide: Read bug, cup, sun, run, hut together. Play 'I spy' with short u things around the house (rug, cup, bus, tub, mug).

questions.q: Which word has short u: cup or cap?
Name a short-u thing you spied.
questions.a: Examples: rug, cup, mug, tub, bus.

days.guide: Read 'Owl Moon.' Then ask who is in the story and where it happens. Your child draws the snowy woods at night and labels two details.

questions.a: A girl (the narrator), her Pa, and an owl.
Snowy woods on a cold winter night with the moon shining.

questions.q: Why do they have to be quiet?
questions.a: To have a chance of hearing and seeing an owl; when you go owling you must be quiet.

days.guide: Your child draws one summer moment, tells it aloud (what happened first and how it ended), then writes one sentence about it while you help stretch out words.

questions.a: One short event, like the time you caught a fish, told with a beginning and an end.

questions.q: What should your sentence start with?
questions.a: A capital letter, and it should end with a period.

days.guide: Your child reads the mixed short-vowel list, then you dictate the 8 spelling words. Finish by having them read their small-moment sentence to a family member.

weeks.assessment_key: Spelling (8): hot, mop, top, dot, bug, sun, cup, run — proficient 7–8 correct. Oral retell rubric: 4 = tells a clear beginning, middle detail, and ending of one moment; 3 = beginning and end; 2 = only a list of events or no ending; 1 = cannot retell.

weeks.prep: Sound boxes and tiles, 20 word cards (4 per vowel: cat, map, bag, ham; pig, sit, lip, win; hot, top, dog, mop; bug, cup, sun, hut; bed, red, pet, ten), 'Henry and Mudge' (first book) by Cynthia Rylant, lined paper, and a 25-word CVC screener plus the 10 sight words from weeks 1–2 plus 'and, to, go, we.'
misconceptions: Confusing short e and short i (bed → 'bid'): /ĕ/ is the 'Ed' sound with a slightly open mouth; practice pairs bed/bid, pet/pit.
Starting every sentence with 'And then': teach first, then, and last as sequence words, and vary them.
Thinking a story with one sentence is finished: ask 'What happened next? How did it end?'

days.guide: Read bed, red, pet, ten, web. Your child segments each in sound boxes and builds it with tiles.
Lay out 5 vowel columns (a, e, i, o, u). Your child reads each of 20 cards and places it in its column, then reads each column aloud.
Read the first chapter of 'Henry and Mudge' together. Ask how Henry feels at the beginning and after he gets Mudge.

questions.q: How did Henry feel at the beginning, and why?
questions.a: Lonely, because he had no brothers or sisters and no children on his street.

questions.q: What did Henry finally ask for that his parents said yes to?
What happened to Mudge as he grew?
questions.a: He grew very big — much bigger than Henry (about 180 pounds in the book).

days.guide: Your child writes 2–3 sentences about a pet or animal, using 'first' and 'then,' and checks each sentence for a capital and period.

questions.q: Which sequence word goes first: then or first?
Check: 'my dog ran' — what is missing?
questions.a: A capital M and a period.

days.guide: Give the phonics screener (25 CVC words and 10 sight words) one-on-one, marking errors. Then your child reads their narrative aloud and adds one detail.

questions.q: Read: fed, pup, lid, jog, nap.

weeks.assessment_key: Screener: 25 CVC words, e.g., sat, man, bad, hit, pin, dig, hot, fox, log, cut, bus, fun, bed, wet, pen, map, lip, rug, top, ten, jam, fit, mud, hen, cob. Proficient = 22+/25 and 9+/10 sight words (the, a, is, I, see, my, and, to, go, we). Narrative rubric: 4 = 2–3 sentences in order using first/then, every sentence with capital and period, an added detail; 3 = in order with 1–2 punctuation errors; 2 = one sentence or out of order; 1 = not readable.

weeks.prep: 'Frog and Toad Are Friends' by Arnold Lobel (library), sh/ch digraph cards, picture cards (ship, shell, fish, sheep, chair, cheese, chick, lunch, bench, shoe), and lined paper.
misconceptions: Reading sh as /s/ + /h/: two letters, one sound — underline the pair and say /sh/ like 'be quiet.'
Mixing ch and sh: /ch/ is a quick sneeze 'choo'; /sh/ is a long quiet sound.
Describing characters only by looks ('Frog is green'): ask what the character does and how he acts.

days.guide: Teach that s and h together make one new sound /sh/. Read ship, shop, fish, dish, shut; your child underlines sh in each.

questions.q: What sound do s and h make together?

days.guide: Read chip, chat, much, chop, lunch. Sort picture cards into sh and ch piles.

questions.q: Does cheese go in the sh or ch pile?
Does shell go in sh or ch?

days.guide: Read 'Spring.' Make two lists: words describing Frog (eager, cheerful, patient, clever) and Toad (sleepy, grumpy).

questions.q: Why does Frog want Toad to wake up?
questions.a: It is spring and Frog wants to play with him.
He wants to keep sleeping and tells Frog to come back about half past May.

questions.q: How does Frog get Toad up?
questions.a: He tears pages off Toad's calendar until it shows May.

days.guide: Reread 'Spring' and look at the pictures of Toad when Frog wakes him. Your child tells how Toad feels and writes one sentence ending with a period.

questions.q: How does Toad feel when Frog wakes him? What in the picture shows it?
questions.a: Sleepy and grumpy — he is in bed, pulling covers or looking cross.

days.guide: Dictate 6 words and one sentence. Then your child tells you how Frog and Toad are different using two details.

questions.q: Describe Frog with two details from 'Spring.'
questions.a: Frog is cheerful and eager; he wakes up Toad and tears the calendar pages.

weeks.assessment_key: Dictation (6 words): ship, fish, shut, chip, much, lunch — plus sentence 'The fish is in the dish.' Proficient 5–6 words and sentence with capital and period. Oral character description: proficient = 2 accurate details, e.g., 'Toad is sleepy — he wants to sleep until May; Frog is lively — he tears the calendar pages.'

weeks.prep: 'Frog and Toad Are Friends,' Venn diagram paper (two overlapping circles), index cards, and a th/wh word list (thin, this, that, path, bath, with, when, what, which, whip, whiz, then).
misconceptions: Reading wh words with a /w/ + /h/ split: wh makes one sound /w/ (in most American speech).
Thinking the voiced th in this and unvoiced th in thin are different letters: same letters, two sounds — feel the throat buzz.
Calling verbs or describing words nouns: ask 'Can you see it, go there, or meet it?'

days.guide: Read thin, this, that, path, bath. Your child puts a hand on their throat to feel buzzing (this, that) or none (thin, path, bath).
Read when, what, which, whip, whiz. Your child writes 3 question words on cards and asks a family member a question with each.

questions.q: Ask a question that starts with What.
questions.a: Example: What is your favorite food?

days.guide: Read 'The Story.' Your child retells, in order, the things Toad does to try to think of a story.

questions.q: Why does Frog want a story?
questions.a: Frog is not feeling well and asks Toad to tell him a story.

questions.q: What did Toad do to think of a story?
questions.a: Walked up and down the porch, stood on his head, poured water over his head, and banged his head against the wall.
Toad feels sick, so Frog tells Toad a story about what just happened, and Toad falls asleep.

days.guide: Teach that nouns name people, places, and things. Read 'A Lost Button' and find 6 nouns; sort them on a chart.

questions.q: Name a person/animal noun from the story.

questions.a: Toad finds his own button on the floor at home, sews all the found buttons onto his jacket, and gives it to Frog.

days.guide: Your child fills a Venn diagram: Frog only, Toad only, both. Then reads the th/wh list.

questions.q: Name one way Frog and Toad are alike.
questions.a: They are both friends who care about each other / both are amphibians who live near each other.

questions.q: Name one way they are different.
questions.a: Frog is usually calm and cheerful; Toad worries or gets grumpy.

weeks.assessment_key: Venn diagram: Proficient = at least 2 likenesses (both are friends, both help each other, both are amphibians) and 2 differences (Frog is cheerful/calm and helps Toad; Toad is sleepy, grumpy, or worried and loses things). th/wh list: proficient 11–12 of 12 read correctly.

weeks.prep: 'Frog and Toad Together' by Arnold Lobel, lined paper, a decodable passage with digraphs (write: 'Chad has a red truck. He packs a lunch and a fish snack. The duck sings on the rock. Then Chad shuts the shed.'), and 5 sentences for noun sorting.
misconceptions: Writing ck after a long vowel or consonant (bakck, milck): ck comes right after a short vowel only.
Writing the ng sound as 'n' (sin for sing): stretch the word and feel the back of the tongue.
Capitalizing every noun: only names of specific people, places, and things (proper nouns) get capitals.

days.guide: Read duck, back, sick, rock, truck. Point out that ck comes right after a short vowel.

questions.q: Which is spelled right: duck or duk?
questions.a: duck — ck comes after the short u.

days.guide: Read sing, ring, long, hung, bang. Your child writes a silly sentence using three -ng words.

questions.q: Write a silly sentence with -ng words.
questions.a: Example: The king sang a long song.

days.guide: Read 'A List.' Talk about why Toad needed his list. Your child writes a 4-item to-do list for tomorrow.

questions.q: Why didn't Toad run after it?
questions.a: Running after the list was not one of the things written on his list.
Toad sits until dark, then writes 'Go to sleep' on the ground with a stick, crosses it out, and they go to sleep.

days.guide: Teach that proper nouns name a special person, place, or thing and start with a capital. Your child writes the names of 5 family members, their street, and town.

questions.q: Fix: 'my sister ana lives on oak street.'
questions.a: My sister Ana lives on Oak Street.

days.guide: Your child reads the digraph passage (count errors), then circles common nouns and boxes proper nouns in 5 sentences.

questions.q: In 'Chad has a red truck,' which noun is proper?

weeks.assessment_key: Digraph passage (37 words): proficient = 34+ words correct (90%). Noun sort sentences (suggested): 1) Sam has a dog. (Sam = proper; dog = common) 2) We go to Texas. (Texas proper) 3) The cat sat on a mat. (cat, mat common) 4) Frog and Toad went to the pond. (Frog, Toad proper; pond common) 5) Mom drove to Lake Tahoe. (Lake Tahoe proper; Mom used as a name = proper). Proficient = all nouns correctly marked.

weeks.prep: Frog and Toad books, bingo cards with sh, ch, th, wh, ck, ng words, paper stapled into a 4-page booklet, and a 20-word digraph check list.
misconceptions: Drawing pictures that don't follow order: number the pages First, Next, Then, Last before drawing.
Writing 'I felt good' with no reason: add 'because...'
Reading digraph words by sounding each letter: remind 'two letters, one sound.'

days.guide: Play digraph bingo: call words (ship, chin, that, when, duck, ring), your child finds and reads each word before covering it.

questions.q: Read: shut, chick, whip, sock, king, path.
questions.a: shut, chick, whip, sock, king, path.

days.guide: Read 'Cookies.' Ask what willpower means and when your child has shown it.

questions.q: What is willpower, as Frog explains it?
questions.a: Trying hard not to do something that you really want to do.

questions.q: What did Frog finally do with the cookies?
questions.a: He gave them to the birds.

questions.q: What did Toad decide to do at the end?
questions.a: Go home and bake a cake.

days.guide: Your child plans a story about doing something with a friend: draws First, Next, Then, Last pictures in the booklet.

questions.q: What goes on the first page?
questions.a: The beginning — who and what you were doing.

questions.q: What goes on the last page?
questions.a: How it ended and how you felt.

days.guide: Under each picture, your child writes one sentence beginning with First, Next, Then, Last, and ends with a feeling sentence.

questions.q: Which word starts the last page?
Add a feeling: 'Last, we ate ice cream.'

days.guide: Your child reads the booklet aloud with expression, then reads the 20-word digraph list.

questions.q: Read: fish, chop, this, what, back, song.
questions.a: fish, chop, this, what, back, song.
Changing your voice to show feelings, pausing at periods.

weeks.assessment_key: Booklet rubric: 4 = 4 sentences in order using First/Next/Then/Last, feeling at the end, all capitals and periods; 3 = in order with 1–2 errors; 2 = missing sequence words or several errors; 1 = incomplete. Digraph check (20): ship, shop, fish, chin, chop, lunch, thin, this, bath, when, what, which, duck, back, rock, sing, long, rang, much, wish — proficient 18+.

weeks.prep: A public-domain 'The Little Red Hen' (e.g., from Gutenberg), stuffed animals, l-blend cards, and a retell checklist (characters, setting, problem, events, ending).
misconceptions: Dropping the second consonant in blends (cap for clap): tap one finger for each sound /c/ /l/ /ă/ /p/.
Retelling just one part: use the 5-finger retell — one finger for each part.
Thinking the hen was mean for not sharing: discuss fairness — the others chose not to help.

days.guide: Blend and read clap, flag, glad, plum, slip, black, tapping one finger per sound.
Read 'The Little Red Hen' aloud. Act it out with stuffed animals, everyone shouting 'Not I!'

questions.q: What did the other animals say each time she asked for help?

questions.a: The Little Red Hen (and her chicks, in some versions) — the others did not get any.

days.guide: Your child retells using five fingers: characters, setting, problem, events, ending.

questions.a: Nobody would help the hen plant, cut, grind, and bake the wheat.
She made the bread herself, and when the others wanted to eat it, she ate it herself.

days.guide: Discuss the lesson: those who help get to share. Your child writes one sentence telling the lesson.

questions.q: What is the lesson of the story?
questions.a: If you don't help with the work, you shouldn't expect to share the reward.

questions.q: Write the lesson in one sentence.
questions.a: Example: People who help get to share.

days.guide: Dictate 8 l-blend words. Then your child retells the story while you score it with the checklist.

weeks.assessment_key: Spelling: clap, flag, glad, plum, slip, black, sled, flat — proficient 7–8. Retell checklist (1 point each): characters (hen, plus the lazy animals, e.g., cat, dog, duck), setting (a farm), problem (no one helps), events in order (plant, cut, grind/mill, bake), ending (she eats the bread herself). 5 = proficient; 3–4 developing.

weeks.prep: Aesop's Fables (Project Gutenberg, e.g., the 1919 Jacobs or 'The Aesop for Children'), r-blend picture cards, drawing paper, and an r-blend passage (e.g., 'The crab and the frog trip on a log. Brad grins and drums. Fran gets a brush.').
misconceptions: Saying 'fog' for frog (dropping r): stretch the blend and have your child watch your mouth.
Thinking a moral is a summary of what happened: a moral is a lesson for our own lives.
Adding -ed and reading every ending as /ed/ (jump-ed): listen — jumped ends with /t/.

days.guide: Read crab, drum, frog, grin, trip, brush. Sort picture cards by br, cr, dr, fr, gr, tr.
Read 'The Tortoise and the Hare.' Discuss why slow and steady won. Your child draws the race with speech bubbles.

questions.a: He was so sure he would win that he stopped to nap, and the Tortoise passed him.
Slow and steady wins the race.

days.guide: Read 'The Lion and the Mouse.' Your child states the moral in their own words.

questions.q: How did the Mouse help the Lion?
questions.a: He gnawed through the ropes of the hunters' net.

questions.q: What is the moral in your own words?
questions.a: Little friends can be great friends; even small people can help.

days.guide: Read jumped, helped, rested. Turn 5 present-tense verbs into past tense to tell what the hare did: run → ran (irregular), nap → napped, laugh → laughed, rest → rested, stop → stopped.

questions.q: Change 'The hare rests' to the past.
Change 'The hare jumps' to the past.

days.guide: Your child reads the r-blend passage aloud, then matches 3 fables to their morals.

questions.q: Match: The Lion and the Mouse.
questions.a: Little friends may prove great friends / kindness is never wasted.

questions.q: Match: The Tortoise and the Hare.
questions.a: Slow and steady wins the race.

weeks.assessment_key: Matching key: Tortoise and the Hare → slow and steady wins the race; Lion and the Mouse → little friends can be great friends (kindness is repaid); The Boy Who Cried Wolf (or the Ant and the Grasshopper, if used) → liars are not believed even when they tell the truth (work now, prepare for later). Passage: proficient 95% words correct.

weeks.prep: A public-domain 'The Three Billy Goats Gruff,' craft sticks and paper for puppets, colored pencils, and a blends check list (stop, snap, spin, skip, swim, smell, nest, hand, jump, milk, tent, best).
misconceptions: Missing the final blend (nes for nest): tap each sound and check the last two letters.
Using 'trips' with plural subjects ('The goats trips'): one goat trips; two goats trip.
Coloring the narrator's words as a character's: only words inside quotation marks are spoken.

days.guide: Read stop, snap, spin, skip, swim, smell. Tap sounds and spell 5.
Read nest, hand, jump, milk, tent. Underline the final blend.

questions.q: What is the final blend in jump?

days.guide: Read the story. Show that quotation marks show talking. Your child colors each speaker's words a different color.

questions.q: What does the troll say when he hears someone on the bridge?
What do the first two goats tell the troll?
questions.a: Wait for my bigger brother, who is much bigger.
The biggest goat butts him off the bridge into the river.

days.guide: Practice 'The goat trips' (one) vs. 'The goats trip' (more than one). Your child completes 6 sentences.
Perform the story with stick puppets, using different voices for the narrator and each character. Then read the blends list.

questions.q: How should the smallest goat's voice sound?

weeks.assessment_key: Puppet show rubric: 4 = clearly different voices for narrator, troll, and three goats, story in order; 3 = some voice changes; 2 = one voice throughout; 1 = could not perform. Verb sentences: 1) The goat trips. 2) The goats trip. 3) The troll yells. 4) The goats eat. 5) The bridge creaks. 6) The brothers run. Proficient 5–6.

weeks.prep: Public-domain 'The Gingerbread Man' and Aesop's 'The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse,' a story map, a 30-word blends list, and lined paper.
misconceptions: Retelling with present-tense verbs: remind that past events use -ed or irregular past verbs (ran, ate).
Comparing by retelling one story then the other: use a chart with the same questions for both.
Thinking the Gingerbread Man is a moral fable: it is a folktale; you can still discuss a lesson (don't trust tricksters).

days.guide: Read 'The Gingerbread Man.' Chant the repeating line and list everyone who chased him.

questions.a: 'Run, run, as fast as you can! You can't catch me, I'm the Gingerbread Man!'

questions.q: Who caught him at the end?
questions.a: The fox, who tricked him into riding on his nose to cross the river and then ate him.

days.guide: Read 'The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse.' Your child tells which home they'd choose and why.

questions.q: Why did the Country Mouse go home?
questions.a: In town the feast kept getting interrupted by danger (people and dogs), and he would rather eat plain food in safety.
Better a simple life in peace than a rich life in fear.

days.guide: Fill a chart: where each character went, the problem, how it ended.

questions.q: Where did the Gingerbread Man go?
questions.a: He ran away from the kitchen down the road to the river.

questions.q: How did the Country Mouse's story end compared to the Gingerbread Man's?
questions.a: The Country Mouse went safely home; the Gingerbread Man was eaten by the fox.

days.guide: Your child writes a 4-sentence fable retelling with first, next, then, finally, in the past tense.

questions.q: Change 'The hare runs' to past tense.
What word begins the last sentence?

days.guide: Give the 30-word blends assessment. Then your child reads their retelling and states the moral.

questions.q: Read: frog, slip, nest, crab, plant.
State the moral of your fable.
questions.a: Matches the fable, e.g., Tortoise and Hare: slow and steady wins the race.

weeks.assessment_key: Blends (30): clap, flag, glad, plum, slip, black, crab, drum, frog, grin, trip, brush, stop, snap, spin, skip, swim, smell, nest, hand, jump, milk, tent, best, sled, frost, plant, crisp, stamp, grand — proficient 27+. Retell rubric: 4 = 4 past-tense sentences in order with sequence words and correct moral; 3 = minor errors; 2 = missing events or moral; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Letter tiles plus an 'e' tile, a storybook and a nonfiction animal book, a T-chart, a National Geographic Kids 'Frogs' book (or similar), and 'short'/'long' cards. Also 6 books for sorting.
misconceptions: Reading cape as 'cap' (ignoring the e): the silent e makes the vowel say its name.
Thinking any book with animals is nonfiction: talking animals with a story = fiction; real facts and photos = nonfiction.
Thinking the final e is pronounced: silent e doesn't make its own sound.

days.guide: Build cap; add e to make cape. Do tap → tape, can → cane, mad → made. Your child reads each pair.

questions.q: What happens when you add e to tap?
questions.a: It becomes tape; the a says its name /ā/.

days.guide: Say 12 words (cap, cape, man, mane, hat, hate, plan, plane, rat, rate, tap, tape). Your child holds up short or long.

questions.q: Is the a in plane short or long?
Is the a in hat short or long?

days.guide: Compare a storybook and a nonfiction animal book. Your child names 3 differences on a T-chart.

questions.a: Fiction tells a made-up story; nonfiction gives true facts. Nonfiction often has photos, headings, a table of contents.

questions.q: Which book teaches you real facts?

days.guide: Read a frog book. Your child asks and answers 3 questions about frog facts.

questions.a: Eggs laid in water; they hatch into tadpoles.
They grow legs, lose their tails, and become frogs.

days.guide: Your child reads 10 a_e words, then sorts 6 books into fiction and nonfiction, giving a reason for each.

questions.q: A book about a pig who goes to school—fiction or nonfiction?
questions.a: Fiction — pigs don't really go to school.

weeks.assessment_key: a_e words: cape, tape, cane, made, game, lake, cave, gate, name, plane — proficient 9–10. Sort: each book correctly labeled with a reason (fiction = made-up story / characters; nonfiction = true facts, photos, labels). Proficient = 5–6 correct with reasons.

weeks.prep: A nonfiction animal book with a table of contents, headings, bold words, and a glossary; sticky notes; animal photos; and an i_e/o_e list (bike, kite, time, ride, five, home, rope, bone, nose, stone).
misconceptions: Reading hope as 'hop': look at the end of the word for e.
Using adjectives that don't describe (The frog is run): adjectives tell what kind, color, size, or how it feels.
Thinking the glossary is the same as the table of contents: the table of contents (front) lists chapters; the glossary (back) explains words.

days.guide: Read bike, kite, time, ride, five. Your child writes each in a sentence.
Read home, rope, bone, nose, stone. Play 'change the vowel': hop → hope, not → note, rob → robe.
Your child uses sticky notes to find the table of contents, a heading, a bold word, and the glossary.

questions.q: Where is the table of contents?
questions.a: At the front of the book.

questions.q: What does a glossary tell you?
questions.a: The meanings of important words, in ABC order, at the back.

days.guide: Look at an animal photo. Your child lists 5 adjectives (color, size, feel) and writes 'The ___ frog is ___.'

questions.a: Example: The small frog is slimy.

days.guide: Your child uses the table of contents to find two facts, then reads the i_e/o_e list.

questions.q: How do you use the table of contents to find facts about what an animal eats?
questions.a: Look for a chapter title like 'Food' and turn to its page number.

weeks.assessment_key: Scavenger hunt: 4 features flagged correctly (table of contents, heading, bold word, glossary) plus two facts found using the table of contents. Word list: bike, kite, time, ride, five, home, rope, bone, nose, stone — proficient 9–10.

weeks.prep: 'Frogs' by Gail Gibbons or another illustrated animal book, index cards, a ReadWorks grade 1 animal passage (free), a main-topic organizer, and a 10-word silent-e spelling list.
misconceptions: Naming one detail as the main topic: the main topic is what the whole text is mostly about.
Thinking pictures are just decoration: diagrams and captions give information too.
Copying whole sentences from books as 'facts': write a few key words on each card.

days.guide: Read cube, tune, mule, these, Pete. Sort mixed silent-e words by vowel.
Read a ReadWorks animal passage. Your child names the main topic and two key details.

questions.a: What the whole passage is mostly about.
An important fact that tells more about the main topic.

days.guide: Look at a diagram and caption. Your child tells one fact learned from the picture and one from the words.

questions.a: It explains what the picture shows.

questions.q: What does a diagram with labels show?

days.guide: Your child chooses an animal and writes 3 facts on index cards from a library book.

questions.a: No — it's an opinion. A fact can be proved, e.g., 'Owls hunt at night.'

questions.q: Where did you find your facts?

days.guide: Give the 10-word silent-e spelling test, then complete the main-topic + 2 details organizer.

weeks.assessment_key: Spelling: cake, game, bike, five, home, rope, cube, tune, these, nose — proficient 9–10. Organizer: main topic (e.g., 'Frogs') plus 2 accurate details from the passage — proficient = both details match the text.

weeks.prep: Fact cards from week 15, a stapled report booklet (cover + 4 pages), crayons, and a 20-word silent-e reading list.
misconceptions: Writing a topic sentence that is a fact detail: the topic sentence tells what the whole report is about.
Fact sentences without capitals or end marks: check each sentence with a finger.
Diagram labels without lines: draw a line from each label to the part.

days.guide: Model a topic sentence: 'Owls are birds that hunt at night.' Your child writes one for their animal.

questions.q: What does a topic sentence do?
questions.a: Tells the reader what the report is about.

questions.q: Write a topic sentence about frogs.
questions.a: Example: Frogs are amphibians that live near water.

days.guide: Your child turns 3 fact cards into 3 complete sentences, each with a capital and end mark.

questions.q: Turn 'eat bugs' into a sentence about frogs.

questions.a: A capital at the start and an end mark.

days.guide: Your child writes a closing sentence and draws the animal with 4 labels.

questions.q: Write a closing sentence for a frog report.
Name 4 labels for a frog diagram.
questions.a: Example: eyes, mouth, front legs, back legs.

days.guide: Your child reads the report to a family member, then adds one adjective to each fact sentence.

questions.a: A word that describes a noun.

days.guide: Your child presents the report aloud. Then give the 20-word silent-e reading assessment.

weeks.assessment_key: Informative rubric: 4 = topic sentence, 3 accurate fact sentences, closing sentence, labeled diagram, capitals/end marks throughout; 3 = all parts with a few errors; 2 = missing a part; 1 = incomplete. Silent-e list (20): cape, tape, lake, game, made, bike, kite, time, ride, five, home, rope, bone, nose, stone, cube, tune, mule, these, Pete — proficient 18+.

weeks.prep: 'A Child's Garden of Verses' (Gutenberg) — print 'Rain' and 'My Shadow,' a poetry notebook, crayons, and an ai/ay list (rain, tail, paint, wait, snail, play, day, stay, gray, tray).
misconceptions: Spelling day as 'dai': ay usually comes at the end of a word; ai in the middle.
Reciting a poem in a flat voice: practice pauses at line ends and stress on rhyming words.
Thinking the shadow in 'My Shadow' is a real person: it is the child's shadow, described playfully.

days.guide: Read rain, tail, paint, wait, snail. Teach 'ai in the middle.'

questions.q: Where do you see ai in a word?

days.guide: Read play, day, stay, gray, tray. Teach 'ay at the end.' Sort ai/ay word cards.
Read 'Rain' and 'My Shadow.' Circle words that help you see or hear something.

questions.q: In 'Rain,' where does the rain fall?
questions.a: On field and tree, on the umbrellas here, and on the ships at sea.

questions.q: In 'My Shadow,' what does the child's shadow do when he jumps into bed?
questions.a: It jumps before him into the bed.

questions.q: Name a word in 'My Shadow' that helps you picture the shadow.
questions.a: Examples: little, 'heels up to the head,' 'like an india-rubber ball.'

days.guide: Begin memorizing 'Rain' (4 lines). Your child copies it into a poetry notebook and illustrates it.
Your child recites 'Rain' with expression. Then give the ai/ay reading and spelling.

weeks.assessment_key: Recitation rubric: 4 = all 4 lines from memory with expression and clear voice ('The rain is raining all around, / It falls on field and tree, / It rains on the umbrellas here, / And on the ships at sea.'); 3 = 1 prompt needed; 2 = 2–3 prompts; 1 = reads instead. ai/ay spelling: rain, tail, wait, paint, play, day, stay, gray — proficient 7–8.

weeks.prep: Stevenson's 'Bed in Summer,' pronoun cards (he, she, it, they, his, her, their), word cards (look, peek, glance, stare; big, huge, giant), and an ee/ea list (tree, feet, sleep, eat, sea, leaf, seed, team).
misconceptions: Using 'him' or 'them' as the subject ('Him ran'): he/she/they come before the verb.
Thinking ee and ea make different sounds: both usually say long e.
Thinking shades of meaning are synonyms that mean exactly the same: they're close but different in strength.

days.guide: Read tree, feet, sleep, eat, sea, leaf. Sort into ee and ea and read in phrases ('a green leaf,' 'sleep in a tree').

questions.q: What sound do ee and ea make?

days.guide: Replace nouns with he, she, it, they in 6 sentences. Then use his, her, their.
Read 'Bed in Summer.' Discuss how the child feels and which words show it.

questions.q: What is the child's complaint in summer?
questions.a: He has to go to bed while it is still daylight.

questions.q: What can he still see and hear from bed?
questions.a: The birds hopping on the tree and grown-up people's feet going past in the street.
It seems unfair/hard; he wants to play ('I should like so much to play').

days.guide: Line up look, peek, glance, stare (and big, huge, giant) from weakest to strongest and act them out.

questions.q: Order big, huge, giant from smallest to biggest.
questions.a: big, huge, giant (huge and giant are both very big; giant is often strongest).

questions.q: What's the difference between peek and stare?
questions.a: Peek is a quick, secret look; stare is a long look.

days.guide: Dictate ee/ea words, complete a pronoun worksheet, and reread 'Bed in Summer' fluently.

weeks.assessment_key: Pronoun sentences (suggested): 1) Ben runs → He runs. 2) Lily sings → She sings. 3) The dog barks → It barks. 4) Mom and Dad cook → They cook. 5) Ana's bike → her bike. 6) The kids' ball → their ball. ee/ea dictation: tree, feet, sleep, eat, sea, leaf, seed, team — proficient 7–8.

weeks.prep: Vowel-team cards (oa, ow, ie, igh), poetry notebook, an orange (or shell/leaf), chart paper, and a word list (boat, coat, road, snow, grow, slow, pie, tie, light, night, high, bright).
misconceptions: Reading ow in snow like ow in cow: ow can say long o (snow) or /ou/ (cow); try both and pick the real word.
Spelling light as 'lite': the igh team spells long i in many words.
Writing a poem with no sensory words: ask 'What did you see, hear, smell, touch, taste?'

days.guide: Read boat, coat, road, snow, grow, slow. Build words with vowel-team cards.

questions.q: What sound does oa make in boat?

days.guide: Read pie, tie, light, night, high. Read 'a bright light at night' three times, getting smoother.

questions.q: What letters make long i in night?

days.guide: Explore an orange with all 5 senses and list sensory words.

questions.q: Name a word for how it smells.
Name a word for how it feels.

days.guide: Your child writes a 5-line senses poem: I see... I hear... I smell... I touch... I taste...

questions.a: Example: I hear the peel rip.

questions.q: Why use sense words in a poem?
questions.a: They help readers picture and feel it.

days.guide: Your child reads the vowel-team list and performs their senses poem.

weeks.assessment_key: Senses poem rubric: 4 = 5 lines, one per sense, with specific sensory words; 3 = 5 lines, some vague; 2 = fewer than 5 lines; 1 = incomplete. Word read (12): boat, coat, road, snow, grow, slow, pie, tie, light, night, high, bright — proficient 11–12.

weeks.prep: Printed 'Jack and Jill' and 'Hickory Dickory Dock,' a vowel-team decodable passage (about 60 words), a timer, a phone for recording, graph paper, and a cold (new) passage for Friday.
misconceptions: Reading fast but skipping words: speed isn't the goal — accuracy and expression come first.
Being discouraged by a 'low' WCPM: compare only to your own earlier score.
Mumbling during performance: practice 'big voice' and looking up at the audience.

days.guide: Read 'Jack and Jill' and 'Hickory Dickory Dock' together with rhythm (clap the beat).

questions.q: In 'Jack and Jill,' why did they go up the hill?
questions.a: To fetch a pail of water.

questions.q: In 'Hickory Dickory Dock,' what happened when the clock struck one?

days.guide: Do three 1-minute readings of the same passage. Count words correct each time and graph them.

questions.q: How do you find words correct per minute?
questions.a: Count words read in 1 minute minus errors.
Practice makes reading smoother and faster.

days.guide: Your child chooses 2 memorized poems and rehearses with gestures and volume.

questions.q: Name one way to show expression.
questions.a: Change voice for feeling, use gestures, pause at line ends.

questions.q: Where should you look while performing?

days.guide: Hold a 'poetry café' — your child performs, you record a video, and each listener gives one compliment.

questions.a: A specific praise, e.g., 'I liked your loud voice in the rain part.'
Listens quietly, looks at the speaker, claps at the end.

days.guide: Give the 25-word vowel-team assessment and a cold passage fluency check (1 minute).

questions.q: Read: train, play, seed, team, boat.

weeks.assessment_key: Vowel-team list (25): rain, tail, paint, wait, play, day, stay, tray, tree, feet, sleep, eat, sea, leaf, boat, coat, road, snow, grow, slow, pie, tie, light, night, high — proficient 22+. Fluency baseline: record words correct per minute; a common mid-grade-1 target is about 25–40 WCPM, but use it as a baseline for growth, not a pass/fail.

weeks.prep: 'Green Eggs and Ham' by Dr. Seuss (library), ar/or picture cards (car, star, farm, shark, corn, horn, fork, storm), and opinion sentence frames ('I think... because...').
misconceptions: Giving an opinion with no reason: always add 'because...'
Confusing an opinion with a fact: an opinion tells what you think or feel; others may disagree.
Reading car as 'cair' or 'ca-r': ar is one bossy-r sound /ar/.

days.guide: Read car, star, farm, park, shark. Write the pattern: a + r = /ar/.

questions.q: What sound do a and r make together?

days.guide: Read for, corn, horn, storm, fork. Sort ar/or picture cards.

questions.q: Which card goes in or: star or fork?

days.guide: Read 'Green Eggs and Ham.' Ask whether Sam's friend should have tried them and why.

questions.q: What does Sam-I-Am want his friend to do?
What happens when the friend finally tries them?
questions.a: He likes them and thanks Sam-I-Am.

questions.q: Should he have tried them sooner? Give a reason.
questions.a: Opinion with a reason, e.g., Yes, because he liked them and wasted a lot of time saying no.

days.guide: Your child writes 3 opinion sentences about foods using 'I think... because...'

questions.q: Is 'Pizza is the best food' a fact or opinion?
Finish: I think apples are great because...

days.guide: Dictate ar/or words, then your child shares an opinion aloud in a complete sentence with 'because.'

weeks.assessment_key: Dictation: car, star, farm, park, for, corn, horn, fork — proficient 7–8. Opinion sentence: proficient = complete sentence with opinion + 'because' + a reason (e.g., 'I think dogs are the best pets because they love to play.').

weeks.prep: A ReadWorks passage about recycling (grade 1), conjunction cards (and, but, or, so, because), irregular word flash cards (said, were, there, could, would), and an er/ir/ur sort.
misconceptions: Spelling bird as 'burd': er, ir, ur all sound /er/ — memorize spelling by word families.
Sounding out irregular words: said doesn't follow patterns — practice it as a heart word.
Using 'and' to join everything: but shows contrast, so shows a result, or shows a choice.

days.guide: Read her, bird, girl, fur, turn, nurse. Teach that er, ir, ur spell the same sound.
Flash-card race with said, were, there, could, would.
Read a short recycling passage. Your child underlines two reasons the author gives.

questions.q: What is the author's main point?
Name a reason an author might give for recycling.
questions.a: It saves resources/trees, keeps trash out of landfills, and can be made into new things.

days.guide: Join sentence pairs with and, but, or, so. Your child writes 4 compound sentences.

questions.a: It rained, so we stayed in.

questions.q: Join: 'I like cats. My sister likes dogs.'
questions.a: I like cats, but my sister likes dogs.

days.guide: Your child sorts er/ir/ur words and tells the author's point and two reasons.

questions.a: er: her; ir: girl; ur: turn.
A fact or idea that supports the author's point.

weeks.assessment_key: Organizer: author's point = we should recycle; reasons from the passage (commonly: recycling saves trees/resources, reduces trash in landfills, things can be made new). Conjunction sentences: 4 correct compound sentences using and, but, or, so — proficient 4/4 with a comma before the conjunction (comma not required for proficiency in grade 1).

weeks.prep: OREO organizer (Opinion, Reason, Example, Opinion restated), two library books (e.g., 'Mercy Watson to the Rescue' by Kate DiCamillo and an 'Elephant and Piggie' book by Mo Willems), and lined paper.
misconceptions: Putting commas between only two items: commas go between items in a list of three or more ('red, blue, and green').
Forgetting the comma between day and year in dates: 'July 4, 2026.'
Choosing a favorite book without a reason from the book: point to a part of the book that supports your opinion.

days.guide: Model a list sentence: 'I like red, blue, and green.' Your child writes 3 list sentences.

questions.q: Add commas: 'I ate eggs toast and jam.'
questions.a: I ate eggs, toast, and jam.

questions.q: How many commas in a list of three things (with 'and')?

days.guide: Write today's date, your child's birthday, and a holiday with a comma between the day and the year.

questions.q: Write today's date with a comma.
questions.a: November 24, 2026 (or the day you teach it).

days.guide: Read two books. Your child chooses a favorite.

questions.q: Which book was your favorite and why?
questions.a: Answer with a reason from the book.

questions.q: Who are the main characters in Elephant and Piggie?

days.guide: Fill the OREO organizer: opinion, two reasons, an example, a closing.

questions.q: What does the O at the end stand for?
Give a reason for liking Mercy Watson.
questions.a: Example: Mercy is funny because she loves hot buttered toast.

days.guide: Your child adds commas in 5 sentences and reads the organizer to a listener.

questions.q: Fix: 'We saw cows pigs and goats.'
questions.a: We saw cows, pigs, and goats.

weeks.assessment_key: Comma sentences (suggested): 1) I like red, blue, and green. 2) We saw cows, pigs, and goats. 3) I ate eggs, toast, and jam. 4) My birthday is May 5, 2026. 5) School starts on September 2, 2026. Organizer: proficient = clear opinion, 2 reasons from the book, 1 example, closing that restates the opinion.

weeks.prep: The completed OREO organizer, editing checklist (capitals, spaces, punctuation, spelling), paper for publishing, and a 24-word r-controlled list.
misconceptions: Revising by recopying only: revising means adding or changing ideas; editing means fixing mistakes.
Reasons without 'because': connect each reason to the opinion.
Spelling r-controlled words like 'shurt': check spelling patterns on the word wall.

days.guide: Your child drafts from the organizer: opinion sentence, two reasons with 'because,' closing.

questions.q: What's the first sentence of an opinion piece?
questions.a: The opinion, e.g., 'I think Mercy Watson is the best book.'

questions.q: What word links a reason to an opinion?

days.guide: A family member asks a question about the piece; your child adds one detail or reason.

questions.a: Changing or adding ideas to make writing better.

questions.q: Add a detail: 'The book is funny.'
questions.a: Example: The book is funny because the pig gets stuck in a hole.

days.guide: Use the checklist to fix capitals, end marks, commas, and r-controlled spelling.

questions.q: Fix: 'i think the girl is smart'
questions.a: I think the girl is smart.

days.guide: Copy neatly, illustrate, and read it aloud as a 'book review.'

questions.q: What should a book review tell?
questions.a: The book's title, your opinion, and reasons.

questions.q: What should you do when reading aloud?
questions.a: Speak clearly, look up at the audience.

days.guide: Give the 24-word r-controlled assessment and score the opinion piece with the rubric.

weeks.assessment_key: Opinion rubric: 4 = clear opinion, 2 reasons using 'because,' closing, correct capitals/end marks; 3 = opinion and 1–2 reasons with minor errors; 2 = opinion with no reasons; 1 = unclear. R-controlled (24): car, star, farm, park, shark, yard, for, corn, horn, storm, fork, born, her, fern, bird, girl, first, shirt, fur, turn, nurse, burn, hurt, perch — proficient 21+.

weeks.prep: 'From Seed to Plant' by Gail Gibbons (library), 2–3 dry beans, a zip bag with a wet paper towel, tape (to stick the bag in a window), life-cycle cards (seed, sprout, plant, flower), and 12 printed words for syllable counting.
misconceptions: Clapping every letter or sound as a syllable: syllables are beats — put a hand under your chin; each time the chin drops is a syllable.
Thinking compound words are any long words: a compound is two real words joined (sun + set).
Thinking a seed turns into a flower right away: plants go seed → sprout → plant → flower → seed.

days.guide: Clap names and objects (Ma-ri-a, ta-ble, ba-na-na). Find the vowel in each syllable.
Read sunset, rainbow, backpack, cupcake. Split them and draw both parts.
Read 'From Seed to Plant.' Start the bean bag and draw it.

questions.q: What does a seed need to sprout?
questions.a: Water, warmth, and air (soil helps the plant grow; sunlight once leaves grow).

questions.q: What carries pollen from flower to flower in the book?
questions.a: Insects such as bees (and the wind) carry pollen.

days.guide: Explain how a seed becomes a flower using the book's pictures. Your child orders 4 cards.

questions.q: What does the flower make so new plants can grow?

days.guide: Your child counts syllables in 12 words and retells the life cycle in order.

questions.a: Seed, sprout (seedling), grown plant, flower, new seeds.

weeks.assessment_key: Syllable sort (suggested 12): cat 1, frog 1, seed 1, sun 1, garden 2, rabbit 2, sunset 2, flower 2, kitten 2, banana 3, dinosaur 3, butterfly 3. Proficient 11–12. Life-cycle sequence: seed → sprout → plant → flower (→ seeds).

weeks.prep: 'The Tiny Seed' by Eric Carle (library), a ReadWorks or Starfall plant passage, a same/different chart, the bean bag, a ruler, and 12 two-syllable words.
misconceptions: Splitting words in the wrong place (ra-bbit): split between the two consonants: rab-bit.
Comparing texts by listing everything: focus on what both say about seeds and what only one says.
Measuring from the wrong end of the ruler: line up the 0 mark with the bottom of the sprout.

days.guide: Split two-syllable words between consonants: rab-bit, nap-kin, kit-ten, muf-fin. Read them.
Read 'The Tiny Seed' and a plant passage.

questions.q: What happens to many of the seeds in 'The Tiny Seed'?
questions.a: Some land on a mountain, in the ocean, or in the desert; one is eaten by a bird; others are eaten by a mouse or trampled.

questions.q: What happens to the tiny seed in the end?
questions.a: It grows into a giant flower, and in the fall its seeds blow away to start again.

days.guide: Make a chart: what both texts say about seeds and what only one says.

questions.a: Seeds need water/soil/sun to grow into plants.

questions.q: What does only 'The Tiny Seed' show?
questions.a: A seed's journey on the wind through many dangers and the seasons.

days.guide: Measure the bean sprout and write a dated sentence in the journal.

questions.a: Example: April 3, 2026: My bean sprout is 2 inches tall.

days.guide: Your child reads 12 two-syllable words and finishes the chart.

weeks.assessment_key: Two-syllable words: rabbit, napkin, kitten, muffin, basket, picnic, sunset, contest, insect, puppet, mitten, tennis — proficient 11–12. Chart: proficient = 2 'both' facts and 1 'only' fact for each text that match the books.

weeks.prep: Word-building cards (roots, -s, -es, -ed, -ing, un-, re-), the sprouting bean, and a short passage with root words (e.g., 'We planted seeds. The plants are growing. I am watering them. Dad replants the beans that fell.').
misconceptions: Adding -s to words ending in x, s, sh, ch: add -es (boxes, wishes).
Thinking -ed always says /ed/: it can say /t/ (jumped), /d/ (played), or /ed/ (planted).
Thinking un- and re- mean the same: un- means not (or opposite), re- means again.

days.guide: Add -s or -es to nouns and verbs: plant → plants, box → boxes, grow → grows. Read in sentences.
Sort -ed words by sound: /t/ jumped, /d/ played, /ed/ planted.

questions.q: What sound does -ed make in jumped?

days.guide: Read planting, growing, watering. Find the root word.
Read unhappy, unlock, redo, replant. Tell each prefix's meaning and draw one.
Hunt for root words in a passage, then a quiz.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz (suggested): 1) fox + es = foxes 2) dog + s = dogs 3) jumped /t/ 4) played /d/ 5) wanted /ed/ 6) root of helping = help 7) unlock = not locked / open 8) redo = do again 9) unkind = not kind 10) reread = read again. Proficient 9–10.

weeks.prep: The bean journal, plant books, and paper folded into a 4-page book plus cover.
misconceptions: Writing pages out of order: number pages 1–4 first.
Copying from the book: write in your own words.
Labels without matching drawings: point a label line to each part.

days.guide: Reread plant books and the bean journal. Your child lists 5 facts about what plants need.

questions.a: Water, sunlight, air, nutrients from soil, and space.

questions.q: Why does a plant need sunlight?

days.guide: Your child writes page 1 (seed) and 2 (sprout) with labels.

questions.q: What part grows first from the seed?

days.guide: Your child writes pages 3 (plant) and 4 (flower/seed) and a closing.

questions.a: Example: Then the seeds can grow new plants!

days.guide: Your child reads the book to a family member and answers questions.

questions.a: Holds the plant in the ground and takes in water.
Holds the plant up and carries water to the leaves.

days.guide: Give the syllables/endings assessment and score the book.

weeks.assessment_key: Book rubric: 4 = 4 pages in order (seed, sprout, plant, flower/seed) with accurate facts, labels, and a closing; 3 = all pages with minor errors; 2 = missing pages or inaccurate facts; 1 = incomplete. Syllables/endings (suggested): rabbit 2, sunset 2, banana 3, cat 1; boxes, played (/d/), jumped (/t/), planted (/ed/), root of replanting = plant, unhappy = not happy. Proficient 9–10.

weeks.prep: 'The Tale of Peter Rabbit' by Beatrix Potter (free on Gutenberg, with Potter's illustrations), a toy for acting out prepositions, a story map, and an ou/ow list (out, house, cloud, mouth, cow, town, owl, down).
misconceptions: Thinking ou and ow make different sounds in these words: both say /ou/ as in ouch.
Saying Peter's problem is 'he ate vegetables': the problem is that he disobeyed and was chased and nearly caught by Mr. McGregor.
Using prepositions without the object (He went under.): say under what.

days.guide: Read out, house, cloud, cow, town, owl. Sort by spelling ou/ow.
Read the first half (until Peter is caught in the gooseberry net). Describe Mr. McGregor's garden using the illustrations.

questions.q: What did Mrs. Rabbit tell her children not to do?
questions.a: Not to go into Mr. McGregor's garden.

questions.q: What did Peter eat in the garden?
questions.a: Lettuces, French beans, and radishes (then he looked for parsley because he felt sick).

questions.q: What did Flopsy, Mopsy, and Cotton-tail do?
questions.a: They were good and went to gather blackberries.

days.guide: Your child tells where Peter went using under, in, through, behind, acting it out with a toy.

questions.q: Where did Peter squeeze to get into the garden?
Where did Peter hide from Mr. McGregor?
questions.a: In a watering can (in the tool-shed).

days.guide: Finish the story. Name Peter's problem and how it was solved.

questions.a: He was chased by Mr. McGregor and couldn't find his way out of the garden.
He found the gate, slipped under it, and ran home.

questions.q: What happened to Peter's jacket and shoes?
questions.a: Mr. McGregor used them for a scarecrow.

days.guide: Dictate ou/ow words; complete the story map.

weeks.assessment_key: Story map: Characters — Peter Rabbit, Mrs. Rabbit, Flopsy, Mopsy, Cotton-tail, Mr. McGregor (also sparrows, mouse, white cat). Setting — Mr. McGregor's garden (and the rabbit-hole home under a fir tree). Problem — Peter disobeys, goes into the garden, and is chased by Mr. McGregor. Solution — he finds the gate, squeezes under, and runs home; he is sick and gets camomile tea while his sisters have bread, milk and blackberries. Dictation: out, house, cloud, cow, town, owl — proficient 5–6.

weeks.prep: 'Little Bear' by Else Holmelund Minarik (library), a short passage with tricky words for self-correcting, and an oi/oy list (coin, soil, boil, boy, toy, joy, point, enjoy).
misconceptions: Spelling boy as 'boi': oy usually ends words; oi is in the middle.
Reading on after a mistake that doesn't make sense: stop and ask 'Does that make sense?'
Guessing unknown words without using the sentence: reread and look for clues around the word.

days.guide: Read coin, soil, boil, boy, toy, joy. Your child writes a sentence with two.

questions.a: At the end of a word.

questions.q: Write a sentence with two oi/oy words.
questions.a: Example: The boy found a coin.

days.guide: Read 'What Will Little Bear Wear?' Describe how Little Bear solves his problem.

questions.a: He is cold in the snow.

questions.q: What does Mother Bear make for him?
questions.a: A hat, a coat, and snow pants.
Mother Bear reminds him he has his own fur coat; he takes off the other clothes and isn't cold.

days.guide: Practice 'Does that make sense?' with a passage. When your child misreads, pause and ask; they reread.

questions.q: What do you do if a word doesn't make sense?
questions.a: Stop, go back, and reread; check the letters and the meaning.

questions.q: 'The horse ran in the house'—does that make sense?
questions.a: No, likely 'horse ran in the field.' Reread.

days.guide: Use the sentence to figure out 5 unknown words and explain each clue.

questions.q: 'The tiny kitten was so minute it fit in a cup.' What does minute mean?
questions.a: Very small; the clues are tiny and fit in a cup.

questions.q: Where do you look for clues?
questions.a: In the words and sentences around the unknown word, and pictures.

days.guide: Read the oi/oy list and do a running record on a passage, noting self-corrections.

weeks.assessment_key: Running record: Accuracy = (words − errors) ÷ words. 95–100% independent level; 90–94% instructional; below 90% too hard. Self-correction ratio: count self-corrections (SC); a ratio of about 1:3 to 1:5 shows good monitoring. Proficient: 90%+ with some self-corrections.

weeks.prep: 'Make Way for Ducklings' by Robert McCloskey and a picture-book version of Andersen's 'The Ugly Duckling' (library), a comparison chart, and a word list (moon, food, spoon, book, look, foot, saw, paw, draw, haul, launch).
misconceptions: Reading oo in book like moon: oo has two sounds — try both and pick the real word.
Saying the central message is 'he became a swan': the message is about not judging by looks or being true to yourself.
Using 'a' before a vowel sound (a owl): use 'an' before vowel sounds (an owl).

days.guide: Sort moon, food, spoon vs. book, look, foot. Read both lists.

questions.q: Which sound does oo make in foot?

days.guide: Read saw, paw, draw, haul, launch. Illustrate three.

questions.q: What sound do au and aw make?

days.guide: Read both stories. Compare the ducks' journeys on a chart.

questions.q: Where did Mr. and Mrs. Mallard decide to live?
questions.a: On an island in the Charles River in Boston, and later the island in the Public Garden.

questions.q: Who stopped traffic for the ducklings?
questions.a: Michael the policeman (with other police officers).

questions.q: What happened to the ugly duckling?
questions.a: He was teased, left home, suffered a hard winter, and in spring found he had grown into a beautiful swan.

days.guide: Your child fills 8 sentences with a/an/the and this/that/these/those.
Read the vowel-sound list and state the central message of 'The Ugly Duckling.'

questions.a: Don't judge others by how they look; everyone can grow into who they truly are.

weeks.assessment_key: Chart: Make Way for Ducklings — Mallards search for a safe home in Boston, ducklings hatch, family walks across busy streets with police help, ends safely in the Public Garden. Ugly Duckling — hatched different, teased, lonely journey through winter, ends as a swan accepted by swans. Central message proficient: 'It's what's inside that matters / don't judge by appearance.'

weeks.prep: A story planner (characters, setting, problem, events, solution), lined paper, and a list of prepositions (under, over, in, behind, through, near).
misconceptions: Story without a problem: ask 'What goes wrong for your character?'
Ending abruptly: tell how the problem was solved and how the character felt.
Run-on sentences joined with 'and then and then': stop with periods.

days.guide: Plan an animal adventure story with a character, setting, problem, and solution.

questions.a: Where and when the story happens.

questions.q: What is a problem in a story?
questions.a: Something that goes wrong for the character.

days.guide: Write the beginning: who, where, and the problem.

questions.a: Example: Once there was a squirrel named Sam who lived in a big oak tree.

days.guide: Write 2 events using next and then, and a solution with how the character felt.

questions.a: Example: Finally, Sam found his acorns under a log and felt happy.

days.guide: Add prepositional phrases for where things happened; fix capitals and end marks.
Give the diphthong/vowel-sound assessment and score the narrative; your child reads the story aloud.

weeks.assessment_key: Narrative rubric: 4 = character, setting, problem, 2+ events with sequence words, solution and feeling, prepositional phrases, correct capitals/end marks; 3 = all parts, minor errors; 2 = missing problem or ending; 1 = incomplete. Diphthong/vowel list (suggested 20): out, house, cloud, cow, town, owl, coin, soil, boil, boy, toy, joy, moon, food, book, look, saw, paw, haul, launch — proficient 18+.

weeks.prep: 2 library books on a topic (e.g., sea turtles), sticky notes, an interview question sheet, and a note sheet with 2 question boxes.
misconceptions: Writing questions that are answered yes/no: start with who, what, where, when, why, or how.
Keeping notes that don't answer the question: cross them out.
Forgetting which book a fact came from: write the book's title on each sticky note.

days.guide: Pick a topic and write 2 questions (e.g., 'What do sea turtles eat?' 'Where do sea turtles lay eggs?').

questions.q: Write a research question about sea turtles.
questions.a: Example: What do sea turtles eat?

questions.q: What words do good research questions start with?
questions.a: Who, what, where, when, why, how.

days.guide: Read two books and jot answers on sticky notes.

questions.a: Depends on species: jellyfish, seagrass, algae, crabs, sponges.

questions.q: Where do sea turtles lay eggs?
questions.a: In nests they dig on sandy beaches.

days.guide: Interview a family member or librarian with 3 questions and ask a follow-up.

questions.a: A new question about something the person just said.

questions.q: How do you show you are listening?
questions.a: Look at the speaker, nod, don't interrupt.

days.guide: Sort notes by question; cross out notes that don't fit.

questions.q: A note says 'Sea turtles have shells.' Does it answer 'What do they eat?'
questions.a: No — cross it out or save for another question.
So each question has its answers together.

days.guide: Your child tells answers using sources and names where each fact came from.

questions.q: Where did you learn that fact?
questions.a: Names the book title or person interviewed.

questions.q: Tell an answer in a complete sentence.
questions.a: Example: Sea turtles lay eggs on sandy beaches.

weeks.assessment_key: Note sheet: proficient = 2 questions, each with at least 2 correct facts that answer it, each fact labeled with its source (book title or person). For sea turtles: eat jellyfish/seagrass/crabs (species vary); lay eggs in nests on sandy beaches; babies crawl to the ocean.

weeks.prep: Poster board, glue, markers, a computer or tablet and printer, notes from week 33, and a smiley-face self-assessment sheet (voice, eye contact, facts).
misconceptions: Statements and questions with the same end mark: statements end with a period; questions with a question mark; exclamations with an exclamation point.
Commands confused with statements: commands tell someone to do something ('Look at the turtle.').
Reading the poster word-for-word with eyes down: practice talking from memory, glancing at the poster.

days.guide: Your child writes a statement, question, command, and exclamation about their topic.

questions.q: Write a question about sea turtles.
questions.a: Example: Where do sea turtles live?

days.guide: With help, your child types 4 fact captions and prints them.

questions.a: Words that tell about a picture.

questions.q: Write a caption for a turtle on a beach.
questions.a: Example: Sea turtles lay eggs on the beach.

days.guide: Glue captions and drawings on a poster with a title.
Your child presents the poster in complete sentences and answers two questions.

questions.q: How should you speak during a presentation?
questions.a: Loud, clear, and not too fast.

questions.q: What do you do when someone asks a question?
questions.a: Listen, think, and answer in a complete sentence.

days.guide: Your child self-assesses with the smiley scale.

questions.a: Answers vary — encourage a specific one.

weeks.assessment_key: Presentation checklist: clear voice, eye contact, 4 accurate facts, complete sentences, answered 2 questions. Sentence types: statement ends with period ('Sea turtles swim.'), question with ? ('What do sea turtles eat?'), command ('Look at the turtle.'), exclamation ('Wow, sea turtles are huge!'). Proficient = all 4 types correct with right punctuation.

weeks.prep: 'Owl at Home' and 'Mouse Soup' by Arnold Lobel, and a 'Poppleton' book by Cynthia Rylant (library), word-category cards.
misconceptions: Defining a word by an example only ('An owl is like Owl'): use category + attribute: 'An owl is a bird that hunts at night.'
Comparing characters by looks only: compare what they do and how they feel.
Reading a chapter too fast: read with expression, pausing at periods.

days.guide: Read 'Tear-Water Tea.' Your child tells how Owl feels and why.

questions.a: He thinks of sad things, cries tears into the kettle, and boils them.

questions.q: Name one sad thing Owl thinks about.
questions.a: Examples: chairs with broken legs, songs that cannot be sung because the words are forgotten, spoons fallen behind the stove, pencils too short to use.

questions.q: How does Owl feel at the end?
questions.a: Happy/content — the tea tastes a little salty but good.

days.guide: Read the story frame of 'Mouse Soup.' Your child tells how Mouse tricks the weasel.

questions.q: What does Mouse tell the weasel?
questions.a: That the soup will taste better with stories.
He tells the weasel to go get the things from the stories (like a bees' nest, mud, stones, crickets, thorns) to add to the soup, and while the weasel is gone, Mouse runs home.

days.guide: Your child reads a Poppleton story independently and records one funny part.

questions.a: A pig who lives in a small town, friends with Cherry Sue (a llama) and others.
Answers vary — check it matches the story read.

days.guide: Sort words from the books into categories and define 3 by category and attribute.

questions.a: An owl is a bird that hunts at night.
A weasel is an animal that has a long body and eats small animals.

days.guide: Compare two Lobel characters, then read a chapter aloud.

questions.q: How are Owl and Mouse different?
questions.a: Owl is alone and a little silly at home; Mouse is clever and tricks a weasel.

questions.q: How are Frog and Toad alike to Owl?
questions.a: Example: all are animal characters in short, funny Lobel stories.

weeks.assessment_key: Comparison: proficient = names one likeness and one difference with story evidence (e.g., Owl is emotional and stays home making tea; Mouse is clever and escapes from the weasel; both are animal characters written by Arnold Lobel). Fluency read: record WCPM and note expression/phrasing; proficient = smooth, mostly accurate, expression at punctuation.

weeks.prep: End-of-year phonics screener (all patterns), a cold grade 1 passage, the week 1 writing sample, the year's writing portfolio, and a summer reading list.
misconceptions: Rushing the screener: assessments are untimed except fluency.
Forgetting capitals in names in the letter: check the greeting and signature.
Using only 'good' and 'nice' to describe: try cozy, bright, noisy, gentle.

days.guide: Give the screener one-on-one, marking errors by pattern (short vowels, digraphs, blends, silent e, vowel teams, r-controlled, diphthongs).

questions.q: Read: ship, frog, cake, rain, star, cow.
questions.a: ship, frog, cake, rain, star, cow.

days.guide: Your child reads a cold passage; retells and answers questions.

questions.a: Characters, setting, problem, events in order, ending.

days.guide: Your child writes a letter to a future first grader with date, greeting, body, closing, signature.

questions.q: How do you write the date?
What goes at the end of a letter?

days.guide: Find words around the house that are cozy, bright, noisy and use them in sentences.
Share the portfolio; compare week 1 and now; choose summer books.

questions.q: What did you get better at in writing?
questions.a: Answers vary; compare: more sentences, capitals, spelling.

questions.q: Name a summer book you want to read.

weeks.assessment_key: Screener: proficient = 90%+ on each pattern; note weak patterns for summer practice. Fluency: end-of-grade-1 benchmark is roughly 50–60 WCPM on a grade-level passage. Letter rubric: 4 = date with comma, greeting, 3+ sentences, closing, signature, capitals on names; 3 = minor errors; 2 = missing parts; 1 = incomplete. Compare to week 1 sentence to show growth.
